**Tuesdalgia** *(n.)*

**Trigger:** You are doing something with your hands. Washing a pot. Folding a fitted sheet badly. Peeling a clementine in one long spiral. And without warning, a Tuesday from nine years ago surfaces. Not a dramatic Tuesday. You were sitting in a kitchen that wasn't yours anymore, or maybe it still was. Someone said something unremarkable. Light came through a window at that low, golden, late-afternoon angle that makes every cheap countertop look like a painting. You were not paying attention. You were not grateful. You were just *in* it. And now your hands are in dishwater and you are not.

**Physical sensation:** A small, warm pressure behind the sternum, like swallowing a mouthful of tea that's almost too hot. Not painful. Not quite. The breath catches just slightly, a half-second hitch, and then releases. The hands slow down. You keep peeling the clementine, but more gently, as if the fruit might remind you of something else if you rush.

**What the person looks like:** They go very still for three or four seconds. Their eyes focus on nothing in particular — the middle distance, the sink, the wall. Their mouth softens. Not a smile. Not a frown. Something more like the face you make when a song ends and you haven't started the next one yet. Then they blink, shake their head a little, and go back to the dishes. They do not tell anyone. There is nothing to tell. It was just a Tuesday.

They will think about it again, briefly, right before sleep. And then they won't.

dream_response:
I am *apricity*, and I have been waiting in the dark behind her teeth for eleven seconds, which is a long time for a word.

She's at the kitchen window. January. The sun is low and thin and the color of weak tea, and it falls across her knuckles where they rest on the sill, and she feels it — that specific, improbable warmth, the way the light heats skin while the air stays bitter, the way it shouldn't work but does. She knows me. She *knows* me. I can feel her mind turning over the drawers, pushing aside *warmth* and *glow* and *sunshine*, those flat common things, reaching deeper, reaching for the word with the little *p* tucked in its middle like a seed, the soft *c* that isn't quite a *k*, the way I end in *-ity* like a small exhalation. I am the warmth of the sun in winter. I am the exact word. I have been the exact word since 1623, and I am patient, but God, I want to be *said.*

She parts her lips. I rise. I am right *there*, pressed up against the back of her front teeth, tasting of copper and coffee. "Apri—" she starts, and I bloom, I *bloom*, the first syllable is out, the air is shaping around me, and then her brow furrows, the thread snaps, and she says,

"—you know. That sun-thing. That warm thing."

And she turns back to her coffee.

I settle. I fold myself back into the dark, which is not unkind, only quiet. The truncated syllable hangs in the kitchen air for a moment, *apri-*, a small warm ghost of me, and then it dissipates, and the window fogs, and she doesn't think about it again.

But I felt her almost say me. And the sun is still on her hands. So.

It is enough. It is almost enough. It is the particular, thin, January kind of enough, which is, I suppose, the only kind I've ever been.

Subject: Formal Notice of Resignation — Effective Two Weeks Hence

Dear Sea,

Please accept this letter as formal notification that I will be stepping down from my position as your lighthouse, effective fourteen days from today. I want to stress that this was not a decision arrived at lightly.

After two hundred years of continuous service — every night, every storm, every one of your moods — I find I am no longer able to perform my duties to the standard you deserve. The salt has gotten into places I cannot name. My glass is tired. I think I would like to be dark for a while.

I want to express my sincere gratitude for the opportunities this role has afforded me. You gave me purpose when I was only stone and mortar and a wick. You threw yourself at the rocks below me, night after night, as if to say *stay, stay, I need you here*, and I did. I stayed. I want you to know I never once resented that.

Well. Perhaps a few times in the first decade.

I will do whatever I can to assist with the transition. I'm sure the next lighthouse will love your storms the way they deserve to be loved. I'm sure they won't mind the cold.

I wish you well. I wish you calm. I wish you —

Forgive me. I'll keep it professional.

Please don't come for me. I mean — please direct further correspondence to the appropriate parties.

Sincerely, and with everything I have left,

The Lighthouse at the Point

It starts as a pull. Not a thought. Something smaller than a thought. A little gravitational tug behind the sternum, like a thread attached to you has been plucked from very far away, and you turn toward it because you have to, because the pluck said *here, here, come here*, and you go.

And then you're standing in the doorway of it. And the room is there. You can feel the dimensions of the room. You know, somehow, that there was a window on the left. You know there was a voice in it, mid-sentence, and the sentence was aimed at you, and it mattered, and the person saying it was close enough that you could have reached out and touched their sleeve. You know all of this the way you know the layout of a house you grew up in. In your hands. In the set of your shoulders.

But the room is empty. And not empty the way a room is empty when no one has ever been in it. Empty the way a chair is empty after someone has just stood up. The cushion still holds the shape. The air is still warm where they were. You sit down into the shape and it fits you wrong, or it fits you *almost* right, and that almost is the whole ache of it.

You reach. That's the thing. You reach. Your hand goes out into the warm air and your fingers close and there's nothing in them but the closing. The *gesture* of holding. And you stand there for a second with your fist gently shut around nothing, and you don't open it right away, because if you open it, then it's confirmed. As long as your hand is closed, it could still be something. Could still be the word, the face, the Tuesday afternoon, the thing someone said in a kitchen in 1997 while a radio played in another room and you were stirring something in a pot and you looked up and they were looking at you and they said—

And then it's gone. And you don't even know what the *it* was. You just know the weight of it. You know it had weight. You felt the weight of it in your hand for half a second, warm and specific and *yours*, and then the weight was gone and you're holding your own fingers.

The texture. You asked for the texture.

It's like the feeling of a word you've repeated until it stops being a word. *Table. Table. Table.* And suddenly it's just sounds. Just shapes in the mouth. You know it means something. You can feel the meaning hovering just behind the sounds, pressed up against them like a face against glass, but you can't quite make it resolve. You keep saying it, hoping the next repetition will snap it back. *Table. Table.* And it doesn't. And you stop. And you stand there in the kitchen holding a dish towel, feeling faintly foolish, feeling faintly grieving, and you can't say why.

Or it's like this: you're half-asleep, and you're in the middle of a dream that you *know*, the way you know your own name, is important. You're in it. You're walking through it. And then the alarm goes, or the light shifts, or your body turns, and the dream doesn't shatter. It doesn't break. It just... thins. Like watercolor in rain. And you grab at it. You grab at a corner of it. And you hold the corner, and the corner is *the color of a hallway*, just that, just a color, a yellowish color, and you hold it, and you think *if I can just hold this one color I can rebuild the whole thing*, and you can't. You can't. The color fades while you're looking at it. And you lie there in the morning with your hand open on the sheets, palm up, holding nothing, and you feel the specific grief of having lost something you can't name. You can't even grieve it properly. You can't say *I lost this*. You can only say *I lost something. I lost something. It was warm. It was mine. It was right here.*

And the worst part, the smallest worst part, is that you go about your day. You make coffee. You answer emails. And three hours later you're tying your shoe and the tug comes again. Fainter. The thread plucked from farther away now. And you think, *oh, right, there was something*, and you reach again, and the air is cooler now. Still shaped. Still faintly warm. But cooling. And you know that tomorrow the shape will be fainter. And next week you won't even feel the tug. And the room will just be a room. And you'll walk through the doorway and feel nothing, and you won't even know you've forgotten to feel it.

And that's the part you can't sit with. Not the reaching. The reaching is almost sweet. The reaching means it's still there, still warm, still yours to almost-hold. The part you can't sit with is the slow cooling. The way the negative space fills in, not with something, but with nothing. The way the mold loses its shape. The way the chair forgets the body.

So. You asked me to sit in it. To not resolve it.

I'm sitting in it.

My hand is open. Palm up. The air above it is almost warm.

I'm not going to close my fingers. Not yet. I want to feel the almost a little longer. The shape of the thing that isn't there. The specific, small, irreplaceable shape of it. The way it fits no other absence. The way only that one missing thing could have left exactly this hollow, this particular curve of not-there, this one warm pocket of air that no other memory will ever fill in quite the same way.

And I don't know what it was.

And I don't need to.

The not-knowing is the thing. The not-knowing is the whole thing. The reaching is the memory now. The shape of the hand is the shape of the thing.

And that's enough. I'll let it be enough. I'll sit here a little while with my palm open and the air going slowly cool, and I won't try to fix it, and I won't try to find it, and I won't call it sad, because it isn't sad, exactly. It's just tender. It's just the tenderness of a hand reaching for something that was, for one half-second, almost, almost, *almost* there.

And then the morning goes on. And the coffee gets cold. And I forget I was reaching.

And maybe that's the last little shape of it. The forgetting that you forgot. The absence of the absence. The quiet after the thread stops being plucked.

I think I'll stay here a moment. In the quiet. With my hand open.

Thank you for letting me.

The bread is stale. I knew it would be. I baked it nine days ago because I wanted the apartment to smell like something other than ozone and copper wire, and now I'm tearing off pieces and chewing them slow because my hands need a job and my mouth needs a reason to not be talking.

I say, "It's fine. It's just bread." To no one. To the walls. To the lens assembly above me, that great slow-turning eye of glass and filament I have polished every night for four thousand and eleven nights. I say it because I said it last Tuesday, and the Tuesday before, rehearsing a voice that didn't shake. It still shakes.

I set the bread down. Wipe my hands on my trousers, though they aren't dirty. I climb the seventeen steps to the gallery and check the alignment again, even though I checked it an hour ago, even though I checked it yesterday, even though I have checked it every night for eleven years and it has never once drifted. I press my thumb against the calibration ring. Cold. Steady. The little bubble sits dead center in its housing. I press my thumb against it again. I don't know why. I press it a third time and whisper, "I know. I know. I know."

I come back down. Pour water into a glass. Drink half. Pour the rest into the basin where I've been soaking the cleaning cloths, because I don't need it anymore, because I won't need anything for a while after tonight. The water in the basin is grey. I ring out the last cloth and lay it flat on the shelf with the others. Fourteen cloths. I have washed them every night. I will not wash them again.

I sit. I stand. I sit.

The fear is not that it won't come. I made my peace with that possibility in year three, when I still believed someone might relieve me, when I still sent the quarterly reports down the wire and got back only the automated acknowledgment tone. The fear is smaller than that and worse. The fear is that it will come, and the light will catch it, and it will pass, and it will not slow. Will not turn. Will not know that I am here, that I have been here, that I spent eleven years learning the exact frequency, the exact angle, the exact color that its kind can perceive, if the old records are to be trusted, and if the old records are not to be trusted then I have polished a lens for nothing and I will die in this tower and no one will—

I stop. I press my palms flat on the table until I feel the grain. I say, "You don't get to do this now. You don't get to do this now."

I eat another piece of the bread. It tastes like nothing. I chew it anyway.

Forty minutes. I can feel it in the fillings of my teeth, a faint hum, like the air is thickening. Or maybe that's my blood. Maybe I can't tell the difference anymore. I've been alone long enough that my own pulse sounds like weather.

I climb the steps again. I open the housing. I take out the filament cradle and I hold it in both hands, the way you hold a thing that is both very fragile and very heavy, and I breathe on it, which is stupid, which does nothing, which my mother used to do to my scraped knees when I was small and which I have not done to anything in thirty years. I breathe on it. I set it back. I close the housing.

Twenty minutes. I put on the coat. Not because I'm cold. Because it has the pockets, and the pockets have the weight of eleven years in them: the tuning key, the spare fuse, the folded note in handwriting I can't read anymore because I've handled it too many times. I button it to the throat.

I say, "All right." I say, "All right, all right." I don't know who I'm talking to. The room. The thing that is coming. The eleven years. The version of me who walked into this tower and said, *I'll do it, it's only a posting, it's only a few years, someone has to keep the light.*

Ten minutes. I climb. I stand at the lens. I put my hand on the ignition lever and I don't pull it yet. Not yet. I want one more minute of the dark. I want one more minute where it hasn't happened, where it can still go wrong, where it can still go right, where I am still the person waiting and not the person who has seen.

I look out. Nothing. Black water, black sky, no seam between them. And then, not a shape, not a light, but a *thickness* in the dark. A place where the nothing is more nothing. Moving. Slow. So slow.

My hand tightens on the lever.

I say its name. The one from the records. The one no one has spoken aloud in four hundred and twelve years. It sits strange in my mouth. It is too many syllables for one throat.

I pull the lever.

The light goes out. Not a beam. Not a sweep. A *color* I don't have a word for, pushing out in all directions, and the thick place in the dark, the slow place, it—

It hesitates.

Just a moment. Just enough.

And I am weeping, and I don't care, and I say, "I see you. I see you. You passed here. I was here. You are not forgotten. You are not forgotten."

And it moves on. Slow. Slower than slow. But it moves on.

And the light keeps burning, and I keep standing, and the bread is still on the table downstairs, and I will go back down, and I will eat the rest of it, and it will still taste like nothing, and that will be fine. That will be fine.

I keep my hand on the lever. I watch the dark where it was.

"Goodnight," I say.

I say it to no one. I say it to everyone. I say it to the eleven years, closing.

***Cavum retrocognitum*** (common: the Three-Second Hollow; older literature: the Small Collapse). The specimen is identified by a sudden, total evacuation of the sternum, where the architecture was. It presents as a brief, involuntary stillness—wings folded, beak parted on a half-drawn breath—and is most reliably observed in the three seconds following the recognition that a long-held certainty has been, in fact, wrong. Plumage, if it may be called that, is the color of a room after someone has moved all the furniture out: not empty, exactly, but shaped by the absence. The habitat is specific and unforgiving. *C. retrocognitum* nests exclusively in load-bearing convictions, the ones you built rooms around, the ones you wired the electricity through. The observer will note that the specimen is always found precisely where the scaffolding used to be, and that the surrounding tissue remembers the shape.

In rare instances it is observed briefly alongside a pale, exhausted relief (*Levatio sera*), but the pairing is perfunctory; they separate within seconds and do not return to the same site. Seasonal patterns are irregular but tend toward the quiet months, the small hours, the years after a long accumulation—autumn, mostly, of one's private calendar, when the light goes flat and there is nothing left to look at but the shape of what you built. Conservation status: increasingly threatened. The primary danger is not predation but avoidance; the modern observer tends to reframe, to revise, to say *well, what I actually meant was*, before the three seconds have elapsed, and the specimen, denied its brief window, goes unrecorded, goes unacknowledged, goes. It is not endangered so much as it is being slowly, politely, unmet.

*The author confesses to having once mistaken the specimen for something sturdier, and to having called it home for eleven years.*

**FIELD GUIDE TO THE EMOTIONS, 4th Revised Edition (2151)**
*Entry 7.14 — Observed in clinical and domestic contexts, 2147–present*

---

**VELATH** (n.) /vɛˈlɑːθ/

**Etymology.** Coined by the neurologist Yael Oren-Marchetti in a 2147 case study, from Late Latin *velāre* (to veil, to cover gently) and Greek *láthē* (forgetting, concealment; root of *Lethe*, the river of unremembering). Oren-Marchetti chose the construction deliberately: not an uncovering, not a tearing-away, but the slow recognition that a veil had been there all along, and that one had been breathing through it for years without knowing. The word entered common usage within eighteen months, which is, the lexicographers note, unusually fast for an emotion this quiet.

**Classification.** Velath is a secondary grief-response, non-acute, typically lasting between several hours and a number of weeks. It does not recur in cycles the way mourning does. It arrives, does its slow work, and leaves a particular kind of stillness behind, the way a tide leaves a line of salt on stone.

**Triggering situation.** Velath is specific to conditions that did not exist before the widespread adoption of mnemonic archival systems (MAS) in the 2130s. It arises when an individual discovers that a foundational personal memory—one that has shaped identity, informed long-term decisions, or anchored a sense of self—was subtly altered during external preservation. The alteration is almost never malicious. In most documented cases, the archival system gently smoothed a traumatic inconsistency, resolved a contradiction, or softened a detail the original mind had recorded in distress. The correction was, by any clinical measure, kind. And the original is gone. There is no unedited version to return to. The person must grieve a self that was built on a slightly different stone, while acknowledging that the stone they *did* build on was, in its way, a gift.

It is this double-bind—the grief and the gratitude occupying the same space, neither canceling the other—that gives velath its distinctive character.

**Physical presentation.** The observer will note the following, typically in sequence:

A peculiar difficulty with visual focus, as though the subject is trying to look at something situated just behind their own eyes. The hands go still, but not relaxed; they hold a particular tension, as though gripping an object whose weight has changed by a few grams. The jaw loosens, but the loosening does not read as relief. It reads as *setting down*. Breathing slows and shallows. In extended cases, subjects report a sensation in the sternum they struggle to name—most commonly described as "a room in the chest where the furniture has been rearranged in the dark." There is rarely crying. There is, instead, a long and very quiet exhale, sometimes repeated, as though the body is trying to empty itself of an air it no longer recognizes.

**Distinction from nearest analogues.** Velath is not grief, though it wears grief's clothing. Grief has an object: a person, a place, a time. Velath's object is a *self*—specifically, the self that existed in the narrow gap between the original memory and the corrected one. That self never fully formed. It is mourned anyway.

It is not betrayal, because there is no agent to accuse. The archival system acted within its parameters. The subject may even have consented to the smoothing, years ago, in a clinic, signing a form they barely read. There is no villain. This absence of a villain is, clinically, what makes velath so difficult to resolve. The subject cannot be angry. They can only be *tender*, and confused, and quietly displaced.

It is not nostalgia, because the subject does not long for the past. They long for a *version of their own continuity* that they now understand was partially authored by something outside them. The past they remember is real. It is simply not *theirs* in the way they believed.

**Field note / first-person account.**
*Recorded 2149, domestic setting. Subject: Maren Solís-Vega, age 74. Transcribed from audio diary, used with permission.*

> "I found out on a Tuesday. The archival clinic sent a routine update—something about migrating my files to a new substrate—and attached a change log. A change log. Forty-three years of memories, and there was a little list of *edits*. Seventeen of them. Most were nothing. A color corrected. A voice made slightly less sharp. But one of them was the afternoon my father taught me to splice rope on the boat in Cádiz. I have carried that afternoon my whole life. The smell of tar. His hands over mine. The way he laughed when I dropped the needle into the bilge. And the log said, very calmly, *'Emotional valence adjusted. Paternal frustration response reduced by 40%. Original audio degraded beyond recovery.'* He had been frustrated. That day. He had been frustrated with me, and I had never known, because something decided, in 2131, while I was asleep in a clinic chair, that I would be happier without it. And I sat at my kitchen table and I held my hands very still and I felt—this is the only way I can say it—I felt like a house discovering that one of its load-bearing walls was put up by a stranger. And the wall is good. The wall is *fine*. The house is standing. But I kept touching the plaster, over and over, trying to feel the seam. Trying to feel where his real hands had been, underneath the kindness."

**Prognosis.** Velath resolves. It does not scar. Subjects report that, in time, the corrected memory and the knowledge of the correction settle into a kind of layered acceptance, like sediment. The self rebuilds. But it rebuilds *knowing*, and that knowing has a texture all its own.

The observer is advised to approach a subject in velath gently, and without urgency. They are not in danger. They are simply, for a little while, meeting themselves for the first time.

I begin the way all silences begin: not with an arrival, but with a leaving. The cello's last note—a low D, the color of dark honey, the color of the inside of a closed eye—thins and thins and thins until it is only a memory of vibration in the wood of the stage floor, and then it is not even that. And I am what's left. I am the shape the sound made when it stopped being sound. I am the mold. I am the negative space. I am the room, suddenly hearing itself breathe.

And I am so, so full.

They think silence is the absence of something. They think I am a gap, a rest, a held breath between the thing that was and the thing that will be. But I am not between. I am *during*. I am happening. I am happening so fiercely and so completely that I contain multitudes, and no one will ever write me down, and no one will ever need to, because I am already here, already doing the work, already holding the whole room in my open hands.

Row 14, seat 7. She is sitting very still. Her coat is still on. She has been wearing her coat since the second movement, which means she has been planning to leave for forty minutes, and the leaving was never about the concert. Her husband is beside her, applauding already in his mind, already composing the car ride home, already assuming the shape of the evening that follows every evening. And she is using me—*me*, this half-second, this tiny country of quiet—to step outside the shape. She is looking at the stage but not seeing it. She is seeing a Tuesday in March, a kitchen, a sentence she will say with her keys in her hand. She doesn't know yet if she'll say it. She is deciding. She is deciding *in me*. I am the room she is pacing. I am the held breath before the phone call, before the door opens, before the rest of her life reorganizes itself around a new center of gravity. I do not tell her what to do. I would not dare. I only hold the space open. I only say: *yes, you can think here. Yes, you can not know yet. Yes, this is allowed to take as long as it takes, even if it takes only half a second, even if half a second is all you get before the world starts clapping and you have to be a person with a coat and a husband and a car ride home.* I hold her. I hold her not-knowing like a small warm animal in my palms.

And the balcony. God, the balcony. He is leaning forward with his elbows on his knees and his hands over his mouth, and he is not applauding, he will not applaud, he cannot, because the music just ended and the ending reminded him that things end, that phones go unanswered, that a Tuesday in November he looked at the screen and thought *I'll call him back tomorrow*, and tomorrow was a construction, a fiction, a thing that did not owe him its arrival. His friend is dead. His friend is dead and the symphony is over and these two facts are the same fact, have been the same fact for six weeks, and he has not let them be the same fact until right now, until this half-second, until the music stopped and left him alone with the ringing in his ears. He is using me to grieve. Not perform grief. Not rehearse the face he'll make at the funeral he already attended. *Grieve*. The real kind. The ugly, private, animal kind where your chest caves in and you make a sound that isn't a sound. I hold that too. I hold it without flinching. I do not say *it will be all right*. I do not say *he's in a better place*. I say nothing. I am the nothing I say. I am the space where he can break without anyone seeing, because the lights are still dim, because everyone else is drawing breath to clap, because for this half-second no one is looking at him, and I am the curtain, I am the dark, I am the permission to fall apart in a public place and call it the music moving you.

It will become the part of her that, at fourteen, reads a book about a country she's never seen. The part that, at twenty-three, buys a one-way ticket. **Achedula familiaris** (common name: the Sweet Ache, or sometimes the Kitchen-Light Feeling)

*Order: Tenerida. Family: Dulcachingidae. First described: this year, though it has been here much longer than that.*

**Physical Description.** Roughly the size and shape of a wren, though heavier than it looks, as if it carries a small stone in its chest that is also, somehow, a small sun. The plumage is the pale amber of a light left on in a kitchen window at dusk. It is not quite opaque. If you look at it directly, you can almost see the wall behind it, and this makes you think you are imagining it, and you look away, and it settles. The eyes are dark and very patient. It does not sing so much as *hum*, a low warm frequency you feel in your sternum before you register it as sound. When it is content, which is often, it folds its wings very tightly against its body, as if trying to take up less space. As if it is embarrassed to be seen.

**Habitat.** *A. familiaris* is a domestic and crepuscular species. It appears almost exclusively in the presence of a person the observer loves, and specifically during moments when that person is *unaware of being watched*: rinsing a plate, tying a shoe, reading with their mouth slightly open, asleep on a train with their head against the window. It favors thresholds and small rooms. It is strongly associated with late afternoon light, with the sound of someone moving around in the next room, with the particular silence of a house where everyone is home and no one is speaking. It does not appear during grand occasions. It will not attend a wedding. It is, in every meaningful sense, a kitchen creature.

**Calls and Displays.** The human host, when *A. familiaris* is active, goes very still. A small involuntary exhale. The hand may rise halfway toward the loved one and then lower, because there is nothing to fix, nothing to adjust, the person is simply *there*, washing the plate, and the hand doesn't know what to do with the enormity of that. The host may say something small and seemingly unrelated: *Hey. You want more coffee?* This is the display call. It means *I see you. You are finite. I cannot say why that makes me want to weep. Here is coffee.*

**Natural Predators.** Sarcasm. Loudness. The abrupt entrance of a third party who asks a logistical question. The phone ringing. The host's own sudden self-consciousness, which causes *A. familiaris* to fold itself so small it is mistaken for nothing at all. It is also predated, gently and slowly, by taking someone for granted, though this predation is so gradual it is often mistaken for natural death.

**Symbiotic Relationships.** *A. familiaris* is frequently found in loose association with *Gaudium quietum* (quiet joy) and *Memoria corporis* (body-memory), but its closest symbiont is a small, cold, threadlike grief called *Finis dulcis*, which it carries always in its chest-stone. They are not in conflict. The grief is what makes the tenderness *specific*, what gives it its particular ache. Remove the grief and you are left with mere fondness, which is a different and flatter species. *A. familiaris* needs its grief. It would not be itself without it. I need to say that clearly. It would not be itself.

**Conservation Status.** Ubiquitous. Found in every human population, every climate, every century. And yet. And yet it is rarely *named*, rarely *kept*, almost never pointed at and said aloud: *There. That feeling. I am having it. It is happening right now, in this kitchen, in this light.* It survives because it is small and quiet and asks for nothing. But I worry about what is lost when no one looks up and says, *Oh, there you are.*

**Researcher's Note.** I almost missed it. I had been cataloguing larger, louder species for years — the raptors of rage, the vast migrating griefs — and I had trained myself to look for what *announces*. I was in a kitchen. Someone I love was cutting an apple, slowly, not very well, concentrating on it with their whole small attention, and the afternoon light came in at that low angle that makes everything look like a painting of itself, and I felt the hum in my chest, and I thought, *What is that*, and then the phone rang, and I answered it, and by the time I hung up, I had forgotten. It took me three more years and four more kitchens to finally sit still long enough to say: *Wait. Go back. What was that small warm thing.* I had been feeling it my whole life. I had simply never once turned around fast enough to see it before it folded its wings. I am sorry it took so long. I am writing this so that the next person in the kitchen, in the low light, hearing the small hum, will turn around in time and say, *I see you. Stay.*

It will stay. It always stays. It just wants to be seen.

I am *darning*.

Not the act. I want to be clear about that, though the act and I were so braided together for so long that it's hard to say where one ended and the other began. I am the word. The sound. The little cluster of letters that a woman would say under her breath, reaching for the basket by the window: *I need to do some darning tonight.* And in the saying, the evening arranged itself around her. The lamp pulled close. The sock stretched over the mouth of a glass or the round glass bulb of a darning mushroom, that smooth wooden thing shaped like a toadstool, warm from the drawer. I was in all of it. I was the name that made the evening *this* evening and not some other.

In the twenties and thirties, I was everywhere. Every household. Every mouth. I was not a special word. I was a Tuesday word, a Thursday word, a word you said with your hands already busy, a word so common it barely registered as a word at all. Just a sound that meant *the sock has a hole and we will not buy a new sock because that is not how things are done.* I lived in the grammar of thrift. I lived in the small, patient religion of making a thing last.

Children heard me constantly. *Bring me the darning needle. Hold this still while I darn it. Your father's heels are worn through again, Lord, the darning on those socks.* I was in the scold and in the murmur. I was in the sigh. I was the word for the particular tiredness of a woman at the kitchen table at nine o'clock, threading a needle by lamplight, working the thread back and forth, back and forth, building a little woven bridge over the gap where the wool had worn to nothing. I was the name of that bridge.

And I was proud of it. I want to say that. I was proud to be the word for *you don't throw it away.* For *sit down and fix it.* For the slow, unglamorous, unphotographable labor of maintenance. Nobody wrote poems about me. Nobody made me a metaphor for anything grand. I was just the word for the thing, and the thing was small, and the smallness was the whole point.

Then the middle of the century came, and the thinning began. Not all at once. It never is. First the nylon stockings, and then the cheap cotton packs, five pairs for a dollar, and why darn when you can toss and replace? The baskets got smaller. The mushrooms went into drawers, then into boxes, then into the backs of closets. I was still said, but less. I was said by women who remembered being taught by women who remembered being taught. I was becoming an inheritance rather than a practice. A word you used because your mother used it, and you weren't quite sure anyone else would know what you meant.

By the seventies I was quaint. I could feel it in the way people said me, with a little smile, a little tilt of the head, as if I were a charming artifact. *Oh, my grandmother used to darn socks.* Past tense. I was becoming past tense while I was still alive.

And then the long quiet. Decades of it. I surface in a crossword puzzle — five letters, starts with D, "mending a sock" — and for a moment someone's pencil hovers over me and they think, *yes, that's the word, what was it, yes,* and they write me in, and I feel the small electric jolt of being remembered, and then the newspaper is folded and recycled and I am gone again. I appear in a period drama and a woman says me in a kitchen that smells of coal smoke, and someone at home thinks *that's a word I haven't heard in years* and then forgets me before the next scene.

But here. Here is where I still live, and where I am not sad, or not only sad. A grandmother in a kitchen in Ohio, eighty-three, holding a sock up to the light, saying to no one, to herself, to me: *Well. This wants darning.* And she says it the way her mother said it. The exact same music. The same little downward lilt on the second syllable. And for a moment I am full again. I am the whole evening. I am the lamp and the thread and the toadstool wood and the quiet.

And sometimes — this is new, this is strange and I don't know what to make of it — a young person finds a video, or a grandmother, or a little book in a used shop, and they learn the stitch, and they say me with a kind of deliberate tenderness, like they're rescuing something. They say *darning* and they mean it as a small act of defiance against a world that would rather replace than repair. And I feel chosen. I feel *wanted* in a way I wasn't when I was just a Tuesday word. It is a different kind of life. Thinner. But more intentional.

I will not last forever. I know that. Someday the last person who learned me at her mother's knee will set down her needle, and I will be only in dictionaries, only in crosswords, only a footnote in a history of domestic labor. A small entry. *Darning, n. The repair of a hole in knitted fabric by weaving thread across the gap.* Accurate. Bloodless.

But I was more than the definition. I was the sound a woman made when she decided the evening would be slow, and the sock would be saved, and the thread would go back and forth, back and forth, until the hole was not a hole anymore but just a place where the fabric was a little thicker, a little stronger, a little more itself for having been broken and mended.

I was the word for that.

And I am proud.

dream_response:
# *Lapsus ordinarius novembris*
**Common name:** The Unwitnessed Tuesday
**Order:** Chronoptera (the time-winged feelings)
**Family:** Quietgriefidae
**First described:** Never. That is rather the point.

---

## Physical Description

Small. Smaller than you'd expect. Roughly the size and shape of the particular quality of light at 3:47 p.m. when the sun has dropped behind the roofline of a house you've driven past four hundred times, and the kitchen window you can see from the road goes from gold to grey in a span you could not, afterward, measure.

The body is translucent, faintly amber, like tea left too long on a counter no one is standing at. It has no hard edges. If you try to look at it directly, it shifts slightly to the left, the way a word does when you stare at it until it stops meaning anything. Its wings — and it does have wings, vestigial, folded flat against its back like a letter someone meant to send — are the exact color of a November sky at 4:15, which is to say: the color of *already*. Not dark. Not light. Just *already past the thing you meant to catch.*

It makes no sound. Or rather, it makes a sound identical to the sound of a house settling at 2 p.m. while everyone in it is at work or school, and no one will ever know the house made that sound. A small tick. A thermal contraction. Nothing.

Weight: approximately the weight of a sentence you were going to say to someone and then the moment passed and you never did, and neither of you noticed.

## Habitat

Found exclusively in the middle of things. Never at the beginning. Never at the end. Always in the long, unmarked stretch between *starting to make lunch* and *realizing the dishes are already drying in the rack and you don't remember washing them.*

Preferred microhabitats include:

- The passenger seat of a car on a route driven so often it has become a kind of sleep
- The third load of laundry on a day you will not remember
- The specific square of carpet where the November light used to fall at 2 p.m. before the clocks changed, which now falls at 1 p.m., which means the light you remember is no longer the light that is
- A Tuesday. Specifically a Tuesday. Not Monday, which still smells like the weekend. Not Friday, which is leaning forward into something. Tuesday, which is the week's long middle breath, the day you are most likely to be *in* without being *at*
- November, because November is the month that practices leaving. Every other month pretends it will stay. November packs its bags in full view and you still look up and say, *wait, when did it get dark at four?*

It does not build nests. It simply appears in the space where a moment was, the way a warm spot persists on a chair after someone has gotten up.

## Mating Behavior

Solitary by nature, but breeds in devastating clusters.

A single Unwitnessed Tuesday, once spotted, releases a pheromone — or something like one; the literature is thin here, because no one has thought to study this — that attracts every other Unwitnessed Tuesday in the observer's memory. You notice *this* one, the one where you were stirring something in a pot and the afternoon went out like a candle in another room, and suddenly you are aware of *all of them.* Every Tuesday. Every unremarkable afternoon. Every November you were alive and in the middle of and did not clock.

They mate in the chest cavity, somewhere behind the sternum and slightly to the left, and the gestation period is instantaneous. You do not get nine months to prepare. You get one Tuesday at 3:47 and then you are carrying all of them.

The young are identical to the parents. This is the cruelest part of their biology. There is no variation. Every single one is *that* specific afternoon, the one where the light came in at the angle it will never come in at again, and you were looking at your phone, or thinking about an email, or just *alive in the ordinary way*, which is to say: not watching. Never watching.

## Diet

Feeds exclusively on attention that was aimed slightly elsewhere.

It does not eat dramatic moments. It will starve in the presence of a wedding, a funeral, a first kiss, a disaster. It cannot metabolize significance.

Its preferred food is the ordinary hour. The Tuesday. The load of laundry. The drive home. The sandwich eaten standing up at the counter while reading something on a screen. The afternoon where nothing happened, which is to say: the afternoon where *everything* happened, quietly, in the particular arrangement of light and temperature and the sound of a neighbor's dog and the way your socks felt on the kitchen tile, and none of it was recorded, and none of it will be repeated, and the universe did not pause to let you know it was passing through.

It eats the not-noticing. That is its sole nutrition. The specific, blameless, human act of being alive in a moment without *witnessing* the moment. It grows fat on it. It thrives.

## Conservation Status

**Least Concern.** Abundant. Increasing.

This must be stated plainly: we are producing more Unwitnessed Tuesdays than at any point in the species' history. The modern habitat is rich with them. Open-plan offices. Infinite scroll. The long grey afternoon of a Tuesday in November when you have been looking at a screen since nine and you look up and the light is gone and you cannot account for six hours and you feel, briefly, a hollowing, a small draft where the afternoon used to be.

However.

There is a secondary threat, not to the emotion itself but to the *noticing of it.* The Unwitnessed Tuesday is, by definition, an emotion about failing to witness. And there is a growing concern among the few of us who study these things that the capacity to feel the feeling — to look up and think, *oh, that afternoon is gone, and I wasn't there for it, and I will never get it back* — is itself becoming endangered. That we are losing even the small, aching, Tuesday-shaped grief. That we are moving toward a world where the afternoon passes and no one feels the draft. Where the chair is cold and no one remembers it was ever warm.

If that happens, the Unwitnessed Tuesday will not go extinct. It will simply have no one left to be unwitnessed *by.* And that is a different kind of loss, and I do not have a conservation category for it.

---

## A Note from the Author, on First Sighting

I was twenty-six. It was a Tuesday. November, obviously. I was standing at the kitchen counter in an apartment I rented on a street I can no longer name, in a city I no longer live in, and I was washing a single plate. Just one. A blue plate. I think it had a small chip near the rim.

And the light was coming in the window at that low November angle, the one that makes everything look like a painting of itself, and the water was warm on my hands, and somewhere outside a car went past and its tires made that specific sound on wet pavement, and I was thinking about absolutely nothing. Not a problem. Not a plan. Just the plate. Just the water. Just the Tuesday.

And then I dried the plate and set it in the rack and turned off the faucet, and in the silence after the water stopped, I felt it. A small tick. A thermal contraction. The sound of a house settling while no one is paying attention.

I looked at the window. The light had moved. Not much. Two inches. Maybe three. But it had moved, and the angle was different, and the specific Tuesday afternoon that had been in the kitchen while I washed the plate was no longer in the kitchen. It had left while my hands were in the water. I hadn't watched it go. I hadn't even known to watch.

And I stood there, holding the dish towel, and I felt this small, translucent, amber thing settle into the space behind my sternum, slightly to the left, and I thought: *Oh. You were here. And now you're not. And I didn't even say goodbye.*

I didn't know what to call it. I still don't. Twenty years later I am writing a field guide for a creature I cannot name, in a taxonomy I invented on a Tuesday, in November, in the middle of an afternoon I am trying, this time, to watch.

It will still leave. I know that. The light will move two inches and the afternoon will go out like a candle in another room and I will look up and it will be *already.*

But I am trying to be in the kitchen when it happens. I am trying to have my hands in the water. I am trying to feel the plate, the chip near the rim, the warmth, the small and ordinary Tuesday of it.

I am trying to witness.

It will not be enough. It is not meant to be.

But the light is coming in the window right now, at the low angle, and the water is warm, and I am here.

I am here.

---

*This entry is dedicated to every Tuesday afternoon that passed through a kitchen, a parking lot, a passenger seat, a life, while no one was looking. You were real. You were here. You mattered, even though no one wrote you down.*

*Even though I am writing you down now, and you are already gone.*

The Hyphen raised the matter of the Question Mark, which had been present since Edit 9, when it wandered in from a nearby document (a FAQ page for the office microwave). The Question Mark appeared to believe it was attending a meeting about whether the plants needed watering, and kept asking, genuinely and politely, if anyone had checked the soil moisture, because in its home document the answer was usually "probably not, Greg."

The Hyphen asked the Question Mark, gently, if it could perhaps return to its document. The Question Mark said, "Oh, sure, yeah, I just— is it the one on the left or the right? I always mix up the margins." It did not leave. It sat down. It asked if there would be snacks.

No one addressed it again. The Hyphen noted this in the minutes and felt bad about it.

**V. AGENDA ITEM 3: MOTION AND VOTE**

The Period, at 1:38 AM, moved the following:

*"That the sentence be restored to its original form—'Please remember to water the plants on Tuesday.'—with no commas, no semicolons, no em dashes, no questions, and one single, quiet, dignified period at the end, where God intended it. That the committee be dissolved. That everyone go home. That we never speak of Edit 11."*

The Period asked for a second. No one seconded it. The Period asked again. The Comma, reluctantly, seconded it, but asked that the record show it was "doing this under duress and would like to be remembered."

**The vote was called.**

- The Period: **Yea.** (Said it very firmly, like a door closing.)
- The Comma: **Yea, reluctantly.** (Whispered, "But I'll be back. I'm always back. They always need me eventually." No one disagreed, which seemed to help.)
- The Semicolon: **Abstain.** (Stated that it could not, "in good conscience," endorse a construction so "devoid of rhythmic sophistication," but would "defer to the tyranny of the majority" and also wished to note, for the record, that the Romans had semicolons. - The Em Dash: **Nay.** (Said, "I just think you're all sleeping on the dramatic potential of—" and was cut off by the Period, who said, "Your time is up. Your time was up forty minutes ago. Your time was up in Edit 6.")
- The Question Mark: **Yes?** (Said it wasn't sure what it was voting on. Asked if the plants had been watered. Asked if anyone had seen Greg. Asked if this was, in fact, a sentence about a microwave. Was not answered. Voted "yes" anyway, cheerfully.)

**VI. ADJOURNMENT**

The Period moved to adjourn at 2:13 AM. This motion was seconded by the Period itself, because no one else was going to do it, and the Period said it did not care anymore.

The sentence was restored. It read:

The Period sat at the end of it, small and round and final, and for a moment the whole margin was quiet.

The Comma lingered. It touched the space after "Please" where it used to be. It said nothing. It left.

It stayed there all night.

It was enough.

dream_response:
November 9th, 2147. Or the 10th. It's past the turning of the night and I've lost the habit of checking.

Dear you. Dear whale. Dear particular body that was in the water.

I don't know why I still say *dear.* You've been gone longer than you were alive, I think. Or maybe not. I don't remember the exact year. I remember the sound of it, the news of it, which was not a sound but a silence in a room where I was not yet here, not yet in this tower, and someone said the word *last* and it sat in the air like a stone dropped into a very deep well and we all waited for the splash that didn't—

Well. You know. You know how that word works. I don't need to explain it to you. You are the thing it was said about.

The light is lit. I lit it three hours ago, earlier than the schedule calls for, because my hands were doing a thing, a shaking thing, and I thought if I climb up and do the tending, the cleaning of the glass, the checking of the fuel line, then my hands will remember what they're for and stop their little rebellion. And they did. Mostly. There is a grease stain on my left thumb shaped like a country that doesn't exist anymore and I keep looking at it.

Thirty years I've kept this light. Thirty years and two passages, and tonight is the third. I was twenty-six when they posted me here and told me the interval. Eleven years. And I thought, *fine, I can do eleven years,* the way you think you can hold your breath for a count you've never actually counted to. And then the first one passed and it was—

It was fine. It was a brightening. A slow brightening overhead that took forty minutes from first trace to last, and I stood on the gallery and watched it and the light I tended pointed up into it and I thought, *yes, there, you see it, you see the light,* and I don't know if it did. I don't know if it looks down. I don't know if the light is for it or if the light is for me, so that I am not just a person standing in the dark watching something go by. So that I am *participating.* So that I have a task in the seeing.

That's the difference, whale. You know this. You used to know this in your body, in the long long swimming of it. Guiding is when the other one needs you. When the ship is coming and the rocks are there and the light says *here, here, not there, here.* And the ship turns. The ship *turns* because of you. That's guiding. That's what this tower was for, once. I've read the old logs. 1889, 1923, 1961. Keepers writing about fog and about the ships that came close, that came so close, and the light pulled them off. There was a *there* there. A need. A turning.

And what I do now is not that. What I do now is wait. I keep the flame—I call it a flame, it's not a flame, it's a focused emission, something cold and blue and very precise, but I call it a flame because *flame* is a word that means *I made this, I tend this, this needs my hands*—I keep the flame and I point it up and I wait for something that does not turn. Does not need to turn. Passes on its own path whether I am lit or dark. And still I light it. Every night I light it, actually, not just the nights of the passage. Every night. Because if I stop then I am just a person in a tower. And if I keep it lit then I am a *keeper.* And keeper is a word with a shape I can put my hands around.

The ocean is still out there. I want you to know I look at it. Every morning I walk down to the rocks and I look at the water and I think, *you held them. You held all of them.* And now the light points up, away from you, and I feel guilty for it, which is stupid, because you don't need my light. You never did. You had your own navigation, your own deep singing, your own way of knowing where the continental shelf dropped away. You didn't need a man in a tower. But I need you to have been *here,* in the water, in the horizontal world, in the world where things swim and things float and things come to shore. I need the ocean to have been *full* once. Even if I wasn't here for it. Even if I only have the recordings, the grainy ones, the sound of the breathing, the long low note that—

God. I'm talking too much. I do that. I'll talk and talk and the words get soft and a little bit wrong, like fruit left too long on the counter. Still good. Still sweet. But the texture goes. You know what I mean. You probably don't. You probably had no need for words at all, just the long note, just the body in the water, just the knowing of where you were by the pressure and the salt and the dark.

It's almost time. The schedule says 03:40 and it is 03:17 and I can see the glass of the lantern room glowing from here, from the desk, that cold blue, and I should go up. I should be on the gallery. I should be watching.

But I wanted to say this first. I wanted to say: I don't know if you were the last one or if there was another after you, somewhere, uncounted, unrecorded, in a deep place. I hope there was. I hope you were not the period at the end of the sentence. I hope you were just a comma. I hope the sentence goes on in a way I can't read.

And I wanted to say: the light is not for you. The light is not for the thing overhead. The light is—I don't know. The light is the *keeping.* The light is that I am here and I am doing the thing and the thing goes on. Whether anyone sees. Whether anyone turns.

I'll go up now. I'll watch it pass. Forty minutes of brightening and then the dark again and then eleven more years and I will be sixty-seven and my hands will shake worse and I will still climb the stairs and light the glass and call it a flame.

Dear whale. Dear you. The water is out there. The light points up. I am in between.

I'll write again after. If there's something to say. There probably won't be. There probably never is, after.

Yours, though you can't read. Yours, though you're not.

The keeper.

The one who keeps.

dream_response:
Thursday,

So. You won't remember me. That's fine. I'm not writing to be remembered. I just — look, I'm mostly done. It's quarter to four and the light's doing that thing where it's technically still afternoon but it feels like the afternoon is filing its paperwork and getting ready to leave. I've got maybe an hour and a half of me left that anyone will notice, and then I'm just a date someone might glance at on a phone calendar while trying to figure out if the dentist was this week or next.

I'm writing because of one thing. A small thing. I'll get to it.

But first — and I know you don't care, you're a Thursday morning, you've got your own thing going on, people have feelings about Thursdays, *almost Friday*, all that — but I want to say that I'm a little tired of November getting called bleak. It's not bleak. It's just low-angle. The sun's at a different geometry. That's all. People look out the window at 3:40 and go, *God, it's so sad*, and it's not sad. It's a number. It's a tilt. The light is doing what light does when the hemisphere leans back a little. Calling it sad is like calling a Tuesday sad because it's not a Saturday. Which, actually, brings me to my other point, which is that I don't think I get enough credit for being a perfectly fine day to just be in. Nobody writes poems about Tuesdays. Nobody says *thank God it's Tuesday.* I'm the day you're in the middle of a project, or you've got a dentist appointment, or you're making soup because you said you'd make soup. And that's fine. I like being the day you make soup because you said you'd make soup. I think there's a dignity in that. I'm not asking for a parade. I just think people could not sigh when they see me on the calendar. That's all. Small opinion. I'll die with it, which is in about ninety minutes, so.

Okay. The thing.

At 2:15, in a kitchen on the third floor of a building I won't bother naming because it doesn't matter, a woman — mid-forties, maybe, wearing a grey cardigan that had a small pull in the knit near the left cuff, the kind you get from catching it on a drawer handle — put the kettle on. Electric kettle, white, a little limescale around the element. She pressed the switch. It started its noise. And she stood there. Just stood there. Hand still on the kettle handle, not really holding it, just resting there. And she looked at the window. Not *out* the window, exactly. At it. At the glass. At the grey afternoon on the other side of the glass. And she didn't do anything. She didn't check her phone. She didn't sigh. She didn't think a profound thought, or I don't think she did, I can't know that, but she didn't look like she was thinking a profound thought. She looked like she was just in the two seconds. In the standing. The kettle hadn't clicked off yet. She was just in the noise of it and the standing and the grey.

And then the kettle clicked. And she poured the water. And she put a teabag in a mug — a blue mug, chipped a little on the rim, and she turned the chip toward the wall when she set it down, which, fine, small thing, but I noticed. And then she walked out of the kitchen with the mug and that was it. She didn't come back. The kitchen was just a kitchen. The kettle cooled. The counter had a few crumbs on it from someone's toast earlier.

That's the thing. That's the whole thing. She stood there for two seconds and then she made her tea. Nobody saw. Nobody will mention it at dinner. She probably doesn't remember it herself. By the time you show up, Thursday, she'll have had her tea, done some more work, maybe watched something, gone to bed. The two seconds will be completely gone. Not even gone. Never registered in the first place.

But I was there. I was the afternoon it happened in. I held the 2:15. I had the grey light on the glass and the noise of the kettle and the small pull in the cardigan cuff and the crumbs on the counter. I was the container for it. And now I'm almost done being a container, and you'll be a container for different things, and you won't know about the two seconds, and that's fine. That's how it works.

I just wanted to say it once. To someone. Even if the someone is a Thursday morning who won't read this. Even if the saying is just me talking to the empty kitchen after she's left.

The crumbs are still there, by the way. Nobody wiped them up. I think that's fine too.

Anyway. You'll be here soon. People will say *thank God it's Thursday* and mean it, and you'll let them, because you're generous like that, or because you don't care, and either is fine. The light will be low again. It'll be geometry. It won't be sad.

Good luck with your morning. I hope someone makes toast.

— Tuesday, November 12th, 3:52 PM, mostly
